quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith
firstReading: Paul recalls that sin had left believers spiritually dead, captive to disordered desires and subject to judgment. Yet God, rich in mercy and acting from immense love, made them alive with Christ, raised them up, and gave them a place with him. Salvation is God’s gift of grace received through faith, not a human achievement, so that believers may live in the good works God has prepared.
psalmSummary: Psalm 100 summons the whole earth to worship the Lord with joy, entering his presence in gladness and praise. The reason for this thanksgiving is theological: the Lord alone is God; he made us, and we belong to him as his people and flock. His goodness, enduring mercy, and faithfulness to every generation make grateful worship the fitting response.
gospelSummary: When someone asks Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute, he refuses to reduce his mission to adjudicating possessions and warns the crowd against every form of greed. Life, he teaches, does not consist in an abundance of goods. In the parable, a wealthy landowner receives an exceptional harvest and plans larger storage so that he may secure comfort for himself. God calls him a fool because his life will be demanded that very night, leaving his accumulated wealth to others. Jesus concludes that the person who stores up treasure for self but is not rich toward God has tragically misunderstood life. The Gospel exposes the illusion that material plenty can guarantee the future and calls disciples to receive life as accountable before God.
saintReflection: Saints John de Brébeuf, Isaac Jogues, and Companions (Memorial): Saints John de Brébeuf, Isaac Jogues, and their companions were Jesuit missionaries and lay collaborators who served among Indigenous peoples of North America and died amid the warfare and upheaval of the seventeenth century. They learned languages, endured severe conditions, proclaimed Christ, celebrated the sacraments, and sought to remain with the communities entrusted to them. Reflection on their mission must acknowledge both their sincere self-offering and the wider colonial history in which Christian proclamation became entangled. The Gospel cannot be imposed by coercion or separated from respect for the dignity and culture of those who hear it. These martyrs' willingness to return after suffering shows radical fidelity to Christ and pastoral charity. Their memorial invites prayer for reconciliation, humility in mission, patient inculturation, and courage to serve without hatred even under severe suffering.
dailyPrayer:
Merciful Father, you loved us when sin had made us unable to give ourselves life, and you raised us with Christ by your grace. Deliver us from the greed that mistakes passing goods for the fullness of life. Teach us to worship you with glad and grateful hearts, knowing that we are your people and belong wholly to you.

Through the intercession of Saints John de Brébeuf, Isaac Jogues, and their companions, give your Church humble courage in proclaiming the Gospel. Purify us of every impulse to dominate, dismiss, or coerce. Grant reverence for the dignity, history, and cultures of all peoples, and lead us in the paths of reconciliation and patient listening. Strengthen those who suffer for Christ, those who serve amid violence and fear, and those who labor to heal wounds between peoples. May we receive each day as your gift, do the good works you prepare for us, and become rich toward you through faith, mercy, and steadfast love. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
Ephesians and Luke disclose the radical priority of God’s gift. Humanity does not rescue itself from sin, death, or the false worship of created things; God makes the dead alive with Christ. Therefore Christian good works are not a means of self-exaltation but the graced path prepared for those who have been received into mercy. Psalm 100 gives this grace its proper liturgical form: joyful adoration, thanksgiving, and confession that the Lord is God and that we are his people.

The rich man in Luke fails precisely at this point. He treats abundance as an enclosed possession and imagines that his future rests in what he has stored. He has no readiness before God, no acknowledgment that life itself is given and answerable to its Giver. To be rich toward God is to live from grace, offer worship, practice mercy, and remain free for God’s will. The martyrs honored today witness this freedom through fidelity, pastoral charity, and endurance. Their memorial also requires an evangelical humility that rejects coercion and seeks reconciliation, so that mission may bear credible witness to Christ’s saving love.
exegesis:
Context: The readings belong together through the question of where human life truly comes from and to whom it belongs. Ephesians begins with an uncompromising diagnosis: apart from Christ, people are dead through sin. Sin is not merely isolated wrongdoing; it is a condition of alienation from God that distorts desire and places the human person under judgment. Against this darkness stands the initiative of God. Because God is rich in mercy and loves humanity with great love, he makes believers alive with Christ. The movement is wholly paschal: death gives way to life, lowliness to being raised up, estrangement to communion. Paul insists that this salvation comes by grace through faith. It cannot be claimed as an achievement, ground for boasting, or possession under human control.

First Reading: Grace does not make human obedience unnecessary. Paul immediately says that believers are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand. The order matters. Good works flow from salvation; they do not purchase it. The Christian therefore acts neither to establish a claim before God nor from passive indifference, but as one newly created for a life that manifests divine mercy. This reading directly corrects the desire to make one’s security rest in anything one possesses or accomplishes. The deepest truth of the believer is not self-sufficiency but baptismal incorporation into Christ’s death and risen life. All faithful service is a grateful participation in the purpose of the God who first loved us.

Psalm: Psalm 100 answers grace with worship. Its summons is universal: all the earth is called to serve the Lord joyfully and enter his presence with thanksgiving. Such praise is not sentiment detached from truth. It rests upon confession that the Lord is God, that he made us, and that we are his people, the flock under his care. This language of belonging is profoundly liberating. We are not self-made, abandoned, or finally possessed by earthly powers. The psalm’s confidence also rests on God’s enduring qualities: goodness, mercy, and faithfulness from generation to generation. In the face of mortality and uncertainty, thanksgiving declares that God’s covenant love remains. The Church’s worship forms hearts able to receive created gifts rightly, neither despising them nor treating them as ultimate.

Gospel: Jesus is approached by a man who wants him to direct a brother to divide an inheritance. Jesus does not deny that disputes about property can be serious, but he refuses the role proposed for him and turns to the spiritual danger beneath the request. He warns against every form of greed, because life does not consist in possessions. The parable then gives this warning a searching shape. A rich landowner’s harvest is abundant, and he decides to enlarge his storage and secure ease for many years. His reasoning is entirely turned inward: his crops, his barns, his goods, his ease. The problem is not the harvest as such, nor prudent care for what has been received. The problem is the enclosed heart that receives abundance without reference to God, neighbor, judgment, or the fragility of life.

Gospel: God’s address to the landowner overturns his imagined control. That very night, his life will be required of him, and his stored goods will pass to others. The parable does not present death as an abstract threat meant to create fear; it reveals the truth that life is a gift entrusted by God and cannot be secured by accumulation. Jesus’ final contrast is decisive: one may store up for oneself, or one may be rich toward God. Richness toward God names a life ordered by faith, worship, mercy, generosity, and readiness to give an account before the Lord. It accords with Ephesians because grace frees believers from the futile project of self-salvation. The person alive in Christ need not build an identity upon abundance, since Christ himself is the source and fulfillment of life.

Saints: The memorial of Saints John de Brébeuf, Isaac Jogues, and Companions gives these readings a demanding ecclesial horizon. Their missionary service and martyrdom witness to a life not held back for self-preservation. They learned languages, endured hardship, proclaimed Christ, celebrated the sacraments, and sought to remain with the communities entrusted to them amid seventeenth-century warfare and upheaval. Such fidelity can be understood as a response to the grace described by Paul: those made alive in Christ are sent to serve in the good works God prepares. Yet their memorial also calls the Church to truthfulness about the colonial history within which Christian proclamation became entangled. Mission cannot be detached from repentance, justice, and reverence for the dignity and culture of those addressed.

Today: The saints’ witness does not authorize domination or coercion. The Gospel of the crucified and risen Lord is offered as truth and love, never imposed through contempt for peoples or their cultures. Their willingness to return after suffering shows pastoral charity and courage, while the Church today is summoned to patient inculturation, reconciliation, and humble listening. Luke’s warning against greed reaches beyond possessions to every attempt to grasp control, status, or religious influence for oneself. Ephesians directs the Church back to her first truth: she exists by mercy. Psalm 100 teaches her fitting posture: grateful worship. On this memorial, Christians may ask for freedom from self-enclosure, courage in suffering, and a missionary charity that serves without hatred. Made alive with Christ, the Church is called to bear witness to him in humility, to honor the peoples she serves, and to entrust every harvest to God.
